paras: The threatened lynching of Herman Schmidt followed the shooting of a saloon keeper's wife in Chico, California, on the night of June 24, 1882. Wire dispatches said a crowd had gathered and that he would probably be lynched before morning, but he was instead tried at Oroville, convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to hang. Later reports drew notice to how quickly the court had disposed of the case.

According to a Chico dispatch in the Sacramento Record-Union, Smidt and his wife had come from Stockton about four weeks earlier and opened a saloon called the "Opera" on Main Street. After repeated quarrels, he was arrested by the City Marshal the week before for assaulting her when she interfered as he beat one of the children. She began divorce proceedings and declined to prosecute him on his promise to leave town, and he was released. The paper added that she was the widow of Professor De Eds of Stockton and the mother of four small children.

About 9 o'clock on the evening of June 24, he was accused of entering the saloon with a pistol and shooting his wife twice from behind, killing her instantly. He ran and was captured several blocks away by officer Carl Goodrich, and at the jail it was found that he had taken poison. A doctor revived him with a stomach pump.

The San Francisco wire version added that while medical aid was being given "the crowd assembled," and that if the poison were counteracted he would "probably be lynched before morning." The fuller Record-Union dispatch mentioned no crowd or threat, and no report of any attack on the prisoner appears in the coverage.

He was examined the following Wednesday, an information was filed in the Superior Court on Thursday, and with assigned counsel he pleaded not guilty. On Saturday, July 1, he was tried at Oroville and found guilty of first-degree murder, in a trial the Record-Union said took two and a half hours. Judge Hundley sentenced him to be hanged on July 6, and he was said to have shown "but little feeling or emotion." No report of the execution was found.

Only the white press covered the case, and the first reports were wire copies that named the accused variously as "Herr Smid," "Herr Snyder" and "Herr Smith." The Los Angeles Herald headed its dispatch "Killed His Wife-Lynching Probable," while the St. Paul Globe called the story "An Ungodly Uxoricide." Shorter versions ran in the "Morning Summary" column of The Daily Gazette on June 26 and in the Cambria Freeman of Ebensburg, Pennsylvania, on June 30, both repeating the expected lynching.

The Sacramento Record-Union, the nearest paper in the coverage, called the killing "most fendish and brutal" and dwelt on the family history rather than any crowd. Its sentencing dispatch praised the court's "promptness" as a "remarkable contrast to the usual procedure of our Courts," and that report was reprinted in Nevada and Montana. None of the reports stated the race of anyone involved.

The crowd and the lynching threat rest on the wire dispatch alone; the more detailed Record-Union account of the same night does not mention them. The accused's name also varies, with the Sacramento trial reports giving Herman Schmidt.

bases: Wire dispatches said a crowd gathered at the Chico jail and the prisoner would probably be lynched, but no attack followed and he was tried and sentenced (A2, A3, A9); no report states anyone's race.

No one was killed by the crowd: the accused was revived from poison, examined, tried and sentenced to hang by the Butte County court (A4, A8, A9); the wire reported only that a crowd assembled and a lynching was thought probable (A2, A3).

The wife's killing, the capture and the poisoning are reported by the San Francisco wire and the fuller Sacramento Record-Union dispatch (A2, A4); the crowd and lynching threat appear only in the wire version (A2, A3, A7), and the Record-Union report does not mention them (A4).

accounts.label: San Francisco/Chico wire
accounts.gist: After the shooting and capture, a crowd assembled while a doctor treated the prisoner for poison, and he would 'probably be lynched before morning' if he recovered.

accounts.label: Sacramento Record-Union Chico dispatch
accounts.gist: A detailed account of the marriage, an earlier assault, the shooting, the capture and the stomach pump, with no mention of a crowd or a lynching threat.

framing.detail: The Los Angeles Herald headed the dispatch 'Killed His Wife-Lynching Probable'; the St. Paul Globe called it 'An Ungodly Uxoricide'.
The Record-Union called the killing 'most fendish and brutal' and later praised the 'promptness' of the court against the 'usual procedure of our Courts'.

conflicts.note: The Sacramento reports, closest to the court, give Smidt and then Herman Schmidt; the wire versions vary.
